steps.body: The general rule covers every case: n × a/b multiplies the count a by n and keeps the piece size b.
steps.narration: The general rule covers every case: n × a/b multiplies the count a by n and keeps the piece size b.

widget.successFeedback: 10/8 — five groups of two eighths make ten eighths, past one whole.
widget.lowFeedback: Your shaded bar is shorter than the target half. Shade more — raise the numerator, or use fewer parts.
widget.highFeedback: Your shaded bar is longer than half. Shade less — lower the numerator, or split into more parts.

commonFractions.feedback: 8/8 is exactly one whole; five groups of two eighths passes it.
2/8 is one group. Five were asked for.

predict.prompt: Does n × a/b ever change the denominator?
predict.reveal: Collecting groups of identical pieces cannot change what a piece IS — only how many you hold.

cml.actionGoal: Collect equal groups of a fraction and watch only the COUNT of pieces change for g4x general.
invariants: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number collects groups of identical pieces: the denominator names the piece size and holds still, while the numerator counts every piece gathered, which is what keeps g4x general a counting problem.
misconceptions: Scaling the denominator along with the numerator, adding the whole number to the numerator, or assuming a product cannot pass one whole.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the denominator DID change when you collected groups, what would happen to the size of each piece?

widget.prompt: Compute 2 × 5/6 as ?/6. What is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplied the whole number by the DENOMINATOR; the piece size stays put and only the count scales.
That is one group's numerator — 2 groups of 5 sixths were asked for.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count the same-size pieces the groups collect; the denominator never changes.

options.feedback: Correct — 6 groups of 3 fifths is 6 × 3 pieces, all still fifths.
That multiplies the denominator, which would make the pieces smaller instead of collecting more of them.
Adding counts one group plus a numerator; 6 groups calls for multiplication.
Scaling BOTH parts renames the fraction without changing its value — that is equivalence, not 6 groups of it.
